en: *Śikṣāsamuccayakārikā*:
When fear and suffering are not dear to me nor to others, what is the distinction of my own self that I protect it and not another? (Śsk 1)
By one who desires to bring an end to suffering and wishes to reach the pinnacle of happiness,
the mind should be made firm in awakening, having strengthened the root of faith.

The restraint of a bodhisattva according to the Mahāyāna consists in reverence for the training; from this, one should know the vital points by which one may remain free from transgression. (Śikṣāsamuccaya 3)

The relinquishment of one's person, enjoyments, and all merit accumulated throughout the three times for the sake of all sentient beings, as well as their protection, purification, and increase. (Śikṣāsamuccaya 4)
One's own body and so forth are given for the enjoyment of sentient beings;
if they are not protected, how can there be enjoyment? What is given that is not enjoyed? // Śsk 5 //

Therefore, for the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings, one should protect one's own person and so forth, by not abandoning virtuous friends and by constantly studying the sūtras. (Śikṣāsamuccaya 6)
In that regard, what is the protection of the personal existence? It is the avoidance of what is harmful.
By what is all this obtained? By the avoidance of fruitless movement.
This is accomplished through constant mindfulness; mindfulness arises from intense devotion;
and devotion is born of fervor once one has understood the greatness of tranquility.
"The Sage has said that one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are;
and the mind does not waver from tranquility due to the cessation of external activity. (ŚSK 9)
By speaking slowly and affectionately, remaining unshakable in all circumstances, one should attract suitable people; thus, one becomes worthy of being accepted.
But the world, having despised that sprout of the Conqueror who is not to be taken up,
shall be cooked in the hells and other realms, like fire covered by ashes.
In the *Ratnamegha*, the Victor has declared this summary of the vow:
one should strive to avoid whatever causes the lack of faith in sentient beings.
This is the protection of one's person through medicines, food, and so forth;
however, by enjoying these out of craving for oneself, a defiled transgression arises.
"One should be one who undertakes good deeds and one who knows the proper measure in all things.
Because of this precept, the protection of his enjoyments is not difficult.
Through freedom from craving for the ripening of one's own self-interest, the wholesome becomes well-guarded;
one should not feel regret, nor, having acted, should one proclaim it.
A bodhisattva should fear gain and honor, always avoid arrogance,
remain serene, and abandon doubt regarding the Dharma.
The enjoyment of a purified body will be wholesome for embodied beings, just as well-prepared food free of husks is for people.
Just as grain covered by weeds withers through diseases and does not flourish,
so too the sprout of a Buddha, shrouded by afflictions, does not attain growth.

What is the purification of the personal existence? It is the cleansing of sins and afflictions through the essential meaning taught by the Perfectly Awakened One; for if one lacks such effort, one goes to the lower realms.
One should practice patience, seek out learning, and thereafter take refuge in the forest;
one should apply oneself to meditative concentration and cultivate the contemplation of the foul and so forth.

One should understand the purification of enjoyments through the complete purification of one's livelihood, and the purification of merit through activity whose essence is emptiness and compassion. (Śikṣāsamuccaya 21)
There are very many takers and this [wealth] is so small; what is the use of it?
Furthermore, as it does not produce complete satisfaction, it must therefore be increased.

What is the increase of the personal existence? It is the cultivation of strength and freedom from laziness. What is the increase of enjoyment? It is the increase of enjoyment arising from generosity that has emptiness and compassion as its essence.
Having first, with effort, made one's resolve and intention firm,
and placing compassion at the forefront, one should strive for the increase of the wholesome.
One should perform the ritual of the *Bhadracaryā*, beginning with prostrations and so forth, with devotion;
one should constantly practice faith and the other [virtues], cultivate loving-kindness, and maintain the recollection of the Buddhas and others. // Śsk 25 //
In all circumstances, the welfare of sentient beings, the unworldly gift of Dharma,
and the thought of awakening are, in brief, the causes for the increase of merit.
Success in the right efforts comes from not being separated from heedfulness,
as well as through mindfulness, clear comprehension, and fundamental reflection.
